definitions.definition: A research program that studies the connections between physics, theology, information theory, and consciousness.
definitions.example: Like studying how the rules of a video game might be related to the story it tells.

definitions.definition: A mapping between two different systems that shows they have the same underlying structure.
definitions.example: Like how a map of a subway system and a map of a computer network can look different but both show connections between points.

definitions.definition: Relating to the Christian doctrine of the Trinity: one God in three persons.
definitions.example: Like how water can be liquid, ice, and steam but still be H2O.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation from a Reformed Christian perspective, emphasizing God's sovereignty and grace.
definitions.example: The belief that God chooses who will be saved, not based on their own actions.

definitions.definition: The view that mathematical truths exist independently of human minds or physical objects.
definitions.example: Believing that the number 2 would still exist even if no humans were around to think about it.

definitions.definition: A method of studying how the same patterns appear in different fields of knowledge.
definitions.example: Looking at how the idea of a 'network' shows up in social media, the internet, and the brain.

definitions.definition: Specific criteria that, if met, would prove a theory false.
definitions.example: Like saying 'if we find a unicorn, my theory about unicorns not existing is wrong.'

definitions.definition: A clear statement of what evidence would disprove a claim.
definitions.example: A scientist saying 'if this experiment shows X, my hypothesis is wrong.'

definitions.definition: A process where someone tries to find flaws in an argument or theory.
definitions.example: Like a lawyer questioning a witness to find holes in their story.

definitions.definition: A proof that shows what a mathematical system can and cannot do.
definitions.example: Proving that you can't divide by zero, no matter how hard you try.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - What I Do Not Claim

definitions.definition: An argument based on the underlying patterns or relationships in a system.
definitions.example: Arguing that two different puzzles have the same solution because they have the same shape.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - What I Do Not Claim

definitions.definition: The idea that you must be open about your own beliefs and assumptions when evaluating others'.
definitions.example: If you criticize someone for believing in God, you should also admit if you believe in materialism.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - The Epistemological Honesty Principle

definitions.definition: Someone who believes that only physical matter exists, not spirits or souls.
definitions.example: A person who thinks thoughts are just brain activity, not a separate mind.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - The Epistemological Honesty Principle

definitions.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies the nature of reality, existence, and the universe.
definitions.example: Questions like 'what is time?' or 'does God exist?' are metaphysical.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - The Epistemological Honesty Principle

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'beginning,' 'origin,' or 'first principle.' Pronounced AR-kay.
definitions.example: In the Bible, 'In the beginning (arche) was the Word.'

definitions.definition: The underlying substance or foundation that something else is built on.
definitions.example: The canvas is the substrate for a painting.

definitions.definition: Something that exists by its own nature, not depending on anything else.
definitions.example: The idea that God's existence is not caused by anything else.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'word,' 'reason,' or 'logic.' Pronounced LO-gos.
definitions.example: In the Bible, Jesus is called the Logos, the divine reason behind creation.

definitions.definition: A mathematical function that produces a sequence of numbers or patterns.
definitions.example: Like a recipe that tells you how to make all the numbers in a list.

definitions.definition: A mathematical expression that describes how order and consistency arise in a system.
definitions.example: Like a formula that calculates how well a team works together.

definitions.definition: A Latin word meaning 'and the Son,' used in Christian theology about the Holy Spirit. Pronounced fil-ee-OH-kway.
definitions.example: The belief that the Holy Spirit comes from both the Father and the Son.

definitions.definition: A mathematical operation that measures how something changes over time.
definitions.example: Speed is the time derivative of position — it tells you how fast your location changes.

definitions.definition: An end point or final goal.
definitions.example: The terminus of a train line is the last stop.

definitions.definition: The way the three persons of the Trinity are related based on where they come from.
definitions.example: The Father is unbegotten (not from anyone), the Son is begotten (from the Father), the Spirit proceeds (from the Father and Son).
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: Not generated or created; having no source.
definitions.example: In the Trinity, the Father is unbegotten — he doesn't come from anyone.
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: Generated or brought forth from another, but not created.
definitions.example: In the Trinity, the Son is begotten of the Father, like a thought from a mind.
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: Coming forth from a source, used especially of the Holy Spirit.
definitions.example: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: The fundamental nature or substance of God.
definitions.example: What makes God God, shared by all three persons of the Trinity.
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: The idea that many different things can be part of one whole.
definitions.example: A team has many players but one goal.
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: Abbreviation for the 'coherence Lagrangian' or a specific mathematical framework in Theophysics.
definitions.example: A tool used to describe how order and unity emerge in complex systems.

definitions.definition: Five key principles of the Protestant Reformation: grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, Scripture alone, glory to God alone.
definitions.example: Beliefs that emphasize God's work over human effort in salvation.

definitions.definition: A mathematical symbol or function that performs an operation on something.
definitions.example: The plus sign (+) is an operator that adds numbers.

definitions.definition: A property where applying an operation twice gives the same result as applying it once.
definitions.example: Multiplying a number by 1 is idempotent — doing it twice is the same as once.

definitions.definition: A property of an operation that changes the size or nature of a system, not just rotates it.
definitions.example: Like cutting a piece of paper (changes it) vs. turning it (just rotates).

definitions.definition: When two operations can be done in any order and give the same result.
definitions.example: Addition commutes: 2+3 = 3+2.
definitions.first_appearance: Section III - The Sign Conservation Theorem

definitions.definition: Mathematical operations that preserve the size or length of a vector, like rotations.
definitions.example: Spinning a basketball doesn't change its shape or size.
definitions.first_appearance: Section III - The Sign Conservation Theorem

definitions.definition: A specific identified isomorphism (structural mapping) in the Theophysics framework.
definitions.example: A numbered finding that links a physics concept to a theology concept.
definitions.first_appearance: Section III - The Sign Conservation Theorem

definitions.definition: A mapping showing that the concept of 'sign' (positive/negative) in physics corresponds to 'grace/fall' in theology.
definitions.example: Like finding that the rules for flipping a switch are the same as the rules for choosing between good and evil.
definitions.first_appearance: Section III - The Sign Conservation Theorem

definitions.definition: The study of salvation — how people are saved from sin and its consequences.
definitions.example: Different religions have different soterologies, like being saved by faith or by good deeds.
definitions.first_appearance: Section III - The Sign Conservation Theorem

definitions.definition: The branch of physics that studies very small particles like atoms and electrons.
definitions.example: The rules that explain how a light switch can be both on and off at the same time (until you look).
definitions.first_appearance: Section III - The Sign Conservation Theorem
